How to Check Your Draft Against a Rubric

UNDERSTAND YOUR GRADING CRITERIA

How to Check Your Draft Against a Rubric

A rubric checker compares your draft with the criteria and performance levels in your grading rubric. RubriCheck helps you see where the assignment meets those expectations, where evidence is missing, and what to revise before you submit.

Check my draft
View pricing

Start with 3 free trial evaluations. Detailed feedback and Strict mode are available with credits or Pro.

What does a rubric checker check?

The rubric defines the review. If it awards points for evidence, organization, and reflection, those are the areas to examine in your draft. A requirement such as a source count or a specific section needs to appear in the rubric or the instructions you provide; the tool cannot infer your instructor's unstated expectations.

Prepare the complete rubric

Include criterion names, point values or weights, and the descriptions for each performance level. Check that an uploaded table has readable row and column headings. Missing descriptors can make the difference between satisfactory and excellent work difficult to judge.

Add the draft you actually plan to submit

Upload the assignment alongside the rubric, or paste both texts into their separate fields. RubriCheck accepts PDF, DOCX, TXT, PNG, JPG, and JPEG files. For images, make sure the text is readable and no rubric rows or assignment pages are cut off.

Use the results to choose your next edit

Read the estimated score range alongside the criteria. Find one unmet requirement, locate the relevant passage, and make a specific change. After revising, check the draft against the original rubric again; a score estimate is guidance for review, not an official grade.

Example: turn a rubric into a draft checklist

Use each performance descriptor to ask a question you can answer with evidence from your draft.

Example: turn a rubric into a draft checklist
Rubric requirement	Question to ask	Evidence to locate
Clear argument	Does my opening state a position that the paper supports?	The thesis and the claims in each body section.
Relevant evidence	Does each major claim have support and an explanation?	A source, example, or result linked to each claim.
Organization	Can the reader follow the reasoning between sections?	Topic sentences and transitions that connect the argument.

Illustrative checklist. Your instructor's rubric determines the criteria and weights for your assignment.

AI Rubric Grader for Assignment Drafts

UNDERSTAND YOUR ESTIMATED SCORE

AI Rubric Grader for Assignment Drafts

RubriCheck is an AI rubric grader that compares your assignment with the grading criteria you provide. Use the estimated score range to identify weaker areas and plan revisions before your instructor gives the official grade.

Estimate my draft's score
View pricing

Start with 3 free trial evaluations. Detailed feedback and Strict mode are available with credits or Pro.

How the AI rubric grader uses your rubric

Provide the scoring rows, available points, and performance descriptions along with your draft. RubriCheck structures the rubric and evaluates the assignment against its criteria. Supplying the complete descriptors gives the review more context than criterion names alone.

How to interpret a score range

An estimated range reflects uncertainty in interpreting the rubric and the work. It is not a measured probability or a promise of your final mark. Read the criterion results before deciding what to change, especially when a rubric uses broad descriptions such as insightful or thorough.

Standard and Strict grading modes

Standard mode provides the regular draft evaluation. Strict mode offers a more demanding review of rubric alignment and is available with credits or Pro. Choose the mode that helps your revision process; neither mode can reproduce every instructor's grading judgment.

When a score estimate needs a closer look

Check the original draft when feedback seems to overlook a passage or interpret a requirement differently. Missing rubric rows, unclear image text, and incomplete drafts can affect the review. Use your instructor's explanations to resolve ambiguity, and keep the final submission in your own voice.

Example: read criterion scores before the total

A total alone does not tell you whether to work on reasoning, evidence, or presentation.

Example: read criterion scores before the total
Illustrative criterion	Estimated points	Revision to consider
Evidence (40 points)	24–29 / 40	Explain how each source supports the main claim.
Analysis (40 points)	25–30 / 40	Connect the findings to the argument instead of only describing them.
Presentation (20 points)	16–18 / 20	Check heading consistency and required formatting.

Invented scoring example, not a product result or an accuracy claim. The possible combined range here is 65–77 out of 100.

Check Your Assignment Against the Rubric

REVIEW ASSIGNMENT REQUIREMENTS

Check Your Assignment Against the Rubric

Use RubriCheck to compare a report, reflection, or written project with its assignment rubric. Upload the draft and grading criteria to see estimated scores and revision priorities while you still have time to make changes.

Check my assignment
View pricing

Start with 3 free trial evaluations. Detailed feedback and Strict mode are available with credits or Pro.

Bring together the rubric and instructions

An assignment brief may contain requirements that are absent from the scoring table, such as a required section or an explanation of your method. Include relevant written instructions with the rubric text so the review has that context. Keep the instructor's original scoring weights intact.

Check reports for method, findings, and interpretation

For a report, locate the passages that explain what you did, what you found, and why the findings matter. A rubric may award separate marks for each. A detailed results section does not necessarily satisfy a separate requirement to interpret limitations or discuss alternatives.

Check reflections for reasoning and specific examples

A reflection often needs more than a description of what happened. Compare your writing with criteria about learning, connections to course concepts, and future action. Point to a concrete experience and explain how it changed your understanding or what you will do differently.

Complete a final submission check

Use the rubric review to prioritize content revisions, then check the actual submission file for the required name, format, attachments, and deadline. RubriCheck evaluates the material you provide; it cannot verify an upload in your school's submission portal or inspect work you have not included.

Example: check a project report for missing requirements

Map each requirement to a specific place in the report before marking it complete.

Example: check a project report for missing requirements
Requirement	What is in the draft	Next action
Explain the method	Lists the steps but gives no reason for choosing them.	Add a short justification for the approach.
Interpret the results	Includes a chart and repeats the values.	Explain the pattern and its relevance to the question.
Discuss limitations	Says the sample was small.	Explain how sample size affects the conclusions.

Illustrative report review. Use the requirements and evidence from your own assignment.

Check Your Essay Against a Rubric

REVIEW YOUR ESSAY BEFORE SUBMISSION

Check Your Essay Against a Rubric

To check your essay against a rubric, compare each grading criterion with evidence in your draft. RubriCheck reviews your essay and your own rubric together so you can identify gaps in the argument, supporting evidence, and structure before submitting.

Check my essay
View pricing

Start with 3 free trial evaluations. Detailed feedback and Strict mode are available with credits or Pro.

1. Upload your essay and the complete rubric

Keep the essay and rubric in their separate input fields. Upload PDF, DOCX, TXT, PNG, JPG, or JPEG files, or paste the text. Include the rubric's performance levels and point values so the check can distinguish a basic response from the standard required for higher marks.

2. Check your thesis and paragraph claims

Find the sentence that answers the essay question and states your position. Then read each paragraph's main claim in order. If the claims drift from the thesis, revise the structure before polishing individual sentences. The rubric may also require a counterargument or a specific type of analysis.

3. Connect evidence to your reasoning

A quotation or citation does not explain itself. For each major claim, identify the evidence and the sentence explaining how it supports the argument. Verify quotations, source details, and citation style against the original sources yourself; rubric feedback is not a substitute for checking references.

4. Revise the highest-priority gap

Use the criterion results and revision priorities to choose your next edit. If analysis carries more marks than mechanics and your draft mostly summarizes sources, deepen the explanation before spending all your time on punctuation. Compare the revised passage with the rubric descriptor again.

Example: check an essay paragraph against the rubric

Suppose the rubric asks for a clear claim, relevant evidence, and an explanation connecting the two.

Example: check an essay paragraph against the rubric
Criterion	Draft evidence	Possible revision
Claim	The paragraph introduces the topic but takes no position.	State the point the paragraph will establish.
Evidence	A quotation appears without context.	Introduce the source and explain why it is relevant.
Analysis	The paragraph ends immediately after the quotation.	Explain how the evidence supports the thesis and address its limits.

Illustrative essay review, not a submitted student's work or a generated evaluation. Apply your own rubric's descriptors.

Rubric Feedback That Helps You Revise

FROM CRITERIA TO PRACTICAL EDITS

Rubric Feedback That Helps You Revise

RubriCheck organizes assignment feedback around your grading rubric. Use it to understand which requirements need attention, connect comments to your draft, and choose a specific next revision before submission.

Get feedback on my draft
View pricing

Start with 3 free trial evaluations. Detailed feedback and Strict mode are available with credits or Pro.

Read the criterion before the comment

Start with the rubric row that the feedback refers to. A comment about evidence can mean that you need another source, a more relevant example, or a clearer explanation of a source you already used. Compare the comment with the descriptor and the passage before deciding what to add.

Turn broad feedback into a visible edit

Replace a vague task such as improve analysis with a concrete action you can complete. For example, add two sentences explaining why the result supports the claim, then discuss one limitation. Each revision should make the rubric requirement easier for a reader to identify in the draft.

Prioritize feedback with the rubric's weights

Fix missing requirements and major reasoning gaps first, especially in heavily weighted criteria. RubriCheck provides a leading improvement priority in the free trial. Credits or Pro unlock detailed criterion feedback and three improvement priorities to help plan a fuller revision.

Review feedback with your own judgment

Check whether a comment is supported by the actual text. If the relevant explanation is already present, improve its clarity or placement only if that will help the reader. You can use feedback in a tutoring discussion, but your instructor's requirements remain the reference for the final submission.

Example: turn a feedback comment into a revision

Keep the criterion, the suggested change, and a final check together as you edit.

Example: turn a feedback comment into a revision
Criterion and feedback	Concrete edit	How to check the revision
Evidence: support is not explained.	Add a sentence after the example linking it to the claim.	Can a reader follow the link without guessing?
Analysis: alternatives are not considered.	Compare a plausible alternative and explain your judgment.	Does the paragraph evaluate rather than just list options?
Structure: the section's purpose is unclear.	Rewrite the topic sentence and connect it to the thesis.	Does the section advance the essay's main argument?

Illustrative feedback and revision tasks. These are examples, not guaranteed comments from an evaluation.

How to Use a Rubric to Check an Assignment

A PRACTICAL SELF-REVIEW GUIDE

How to Use a Rubric to Check an Assignment

Use a rubric as a checklist for the evidence your assignment needs to contain. Read the criteria, find supporting passages in your draft, compare them with the performance descriptions, and revise the largest gaps before submission.

Review my draft with RubriCheck
View pricing

Start with 3 free trial evaluations. Detailed feedback and Strict mode are available with credits or Pro.

Step 1: Separate criteria, levels, and weights

Criteria describe what is assessed, such as analysis or use of evidence. Performance levels describe how well you must demonstrate it, and weights indicate its share of the grade. Copy each criterion into a checklist and keep its highest-level descriptor beside it so you can review them together.

Step 2: Locate evidence in the draft

For each criterion, record a paragraph, section, or figure that demonstrates it. Avoid marking a row complete just because you mentioned the topic. If the rubric says evaluate two approaches, look for an actual comparison and judgment about those approaches, not two separate descriptions.

Step 3: Choose a level and explain why

Compare the passage with the full descriptor at each level. Record both what meets the standard and what is missing. When your draft sits between two levels, write down the uncertainty instead of automatically choosing the higher score; that gap can become a useful revision task.

Step 4: Prioritize, revise, and check again

Start with missing requirements and substantial weaknesses in heavily weighted criteria. Convert each gap into a specific edit, such as explaining a limitation or connecting evidence to a claim. After revision, repeat the checklist and confirm that the final file satisfies the assignment instructions.

Worked example: choose the next revision

In this invented 100-point rubric, analysis and evidence carry most of the marks. The notes turn a broad self-rating into edits you can make.

Worked example: choose the next revision
Criterion and weight	Self-check evidence	Revision decision
Analysis — 40%	Describes two approaches but does not compare them.	Add a comparison using the same measures for both approaches.
Evidence — 35%	Sources support the first approach only.	Find relevant support for the second approach and explain it.
Organization — 25%	Sections follow a clear order; one transition is abrupt.	Add a transition after addressing analysis and evidence.

Illustrative weights, not a universal marking scheme. You can use this process manually or use RubriCheck to assist the review.

Privacy Policy

Last updated: February 26, 2026. This Privacy Policy explains what information RubriCheck processes, why we process it, and the choices available to you.

RubriCheck does not sell personal information. Access to user data is restricted to authorized systems and personnel for security, support, and product operations.

Information We Process

Depending on usage, we may process rubric text, assignment text, uploaded files, evaluation outputs, account email, entitlement status, payment session metadata, and anti-abuse telemetry such as IP-derived usage counters.

How We Use Information

We use data to deliver grading and rewrite suggestion features, enforce free and paid limits, prevent abuse, troubleshoot issues, and maintain service performance and security.

Payments and Billing

Billing is handled through third-party processors. RubriCheck stores only the minimum billing-related data needed to reconcile entitlements and support account recovery. Full payment card details are not stored by RubriCheck.

Data Sharing

Data may be shared with trusted service providers that support hosting, analytics, AI processing, and payments under contractual obligations. Data may also be disclosed where required by law or to protect users and service integrity.

Your Choices

You may request access, correction, or deletion of eligible personal data. Some records may be retained as required for legal, accounting, fraud prevention, or security reasons.

Contact

For privacy requests, use the support channel listed on the product site and include the email associated with your account.

Data Retention Policy

Last updated: February 26, 2026. This policy summarizes default retention windows for RubriCheck data categories.

Actual retention may vary by legal obligations, fraud prevention needs, and incident response requirements.

Evaluation Data

Rubric inputs, assignment inputs, and generated outputs are generally retained for up to 30 days for abuse monitoring, troubleshooting, and quality review, unless a shorter or longer period is required for security or legal reasons.

Usage and Security Logs

Technical logs and rate-limit counters may be retained for operational security, reliability analysis, and abuse detection, then deleted or anonymized according to system policies.

Billing and Entitlement Records

Subscription, top-up, and entitlement records are retained for the period needed for accounting, tax, chargeback handling, and legal compliance.

Deletion Requests

You can request deletion of eligible personal data through support. Some records may be excluded from deletion where retention is required by law, fraud prevention, or legitimate security interests.
